For application files, the rubric only fails a file that has HTTP or transport items in a method or function signature, or that throws them. That means requests, responses, HTTP context, status codes or HTTP errors. This file has none of these. Its public methods take only primitives (title: string, capacity: number, id: string). They return Promise<Course> or Promise<Course[]>, and Course is a domain type. The only thing it throws is the project's own DomainError, not an HTTP exception. The rubric bans framework types, ORM types, decorators and direct I/O only in domain files, so @Injectable and the ORM-backed persistence are allowed here. The constructor injects a TypeORM Repository<CourseEntity> with @InjectRepository. CourseEntity is in the infrastructure layer, which the application layer may depend on, so this counts as dependency wiring. The capacity check (1 to 300) and the publish decision are business rules, and the application layer may own them. No candidate flags were raised, and I found no other violation.
